Before you read this map of who has electricity, read the definition it uses: a source that can provide very basic lighting and charge a phone or run a radio for four hours a day. That's the bar.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Four hours of a radio. Anything above that counts as access, which means the pale countries here include millions of households that would not describe their own electricity supply as reliable.

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)
2/ Even against that low standard, somewhere between 685 and 750 million people fall below it, depending on which agency you ask. About four in five of them live in Sub-Saharan Africa.

3/ The darkest countries are under 30%: Chad, the Central African Republic, South Sudan, Burundi, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Papua New Guinea. In the DRC most of the population has no grid connection at all.

4/ The DRC is the cruellest case on the map. The Congo River is one of the great hydroelectric sites on Earth and the Inga dams already sit on it — but that capacity was built largely to power mining, not households.

5/ North Korea is the outlier that isn't about resources. Its neighbours are at effectively 100%; it sits in a band closer to Central Africa's. The map is catching an infrastructure collapse, not a country that never built one.

6/ India is the success story the map hides by rendering it pale. In 2000 several hundred million Indians had no electricity. Near-universal household access arrived inside about two decades — the fastest rollout in history.

7/ Which is why the definition matters. Access on this map is the difference between a dark house and a lit one. It is not the difference between a lit house and a modern economy.
